aspects.says: ConcurrentHashMap's methods never lock the map object, so synchronized on the map excludes only code that takes the same lock.
basis: section:Design Note: Why a ConcurrentHashMap Can't Be Locked From Outside
aspects.reason: a fact of the design note and reference table, shown by one call; a deterministic test could only repeat it

aspects.says: CopyOnWriteArrayList copies the whole array on every write, so it suits lists read far more often than written; its walks never wait for a writer and never throw.
basis: section:CopyOnWriteArrayList Copies the Whole Array on Every Write

aspects.says: A synchronized wrapper, like a ConcurrentHashMap, makes each call atomic but not a get followed by a put; a read-modify-write must be one call such as merge or compute.
basis: section:A Synchronized Wrapper Makes Each Call Atomic, Not a Sequence of Calls

aspects.says: A concurrent map makes finding or creating an entry atomic, not later changes to the object stored in it; computeIfAbsent creates a missing value once, a shared value needs its own thread safety, and a change that must agree with the entry being there goes inside compute.
basis: section:A Thread-Safe Map Guards Its Entries, Not the Objects Stored in Them

aspects.says: A plain HashMap written by several threads loses entries even when no key is written twice, and can throw or never return from put(), because the threads share its table.
basis: section:A Plain HashMap Shared by Writers Loses Entries and Can Hang

aspects.says: ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys and values, its size() is a transient value while others write, and a computeIfAbsent function that updates the same key throws IllegalStateException.
aspects.reason: lookup facts in the reference table, each shown by one call; nothing to reason about that a practice could grade beyond repeating the table

aspects.says: computeIfAbsent followed by add on a plain ArrayList value loses elements and can throw, because the add runs after the map's atomic call.
basis: section:A Thread-Safe Map Guards Its Entries, Not the Objects Stored in Them

aspects.says: Walking a synchronized wrapper is many calls; the walk holds the wrapper's own lock throughout, and every writer waits for it.
basis: section:Walking a Wrapper Is Many Calls: Hold the Wrapper's Lock for the Whole Walk
